1.sense: The Prophet is confronted with his own choice: something Allah had made lawful, put out of reach by his own words, in order to keep peace with a wife. The question "why" is not a request for information; it names the trade he made, law weighed against a wife's contentment, and marks that the exchange did not need to happen. Allah closes the verse on forgiveness and mercy before any fault is specified.

notes.t: The setting classical exegesis gives is an evening the Prophet stayed longer than usual at Zaynab bint Jahsh's rooms drinking honey; two of his wives arranged to tell him his breath smelled of a bitter gum, so he swore off the honey, and this verse questions that oath.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Divorce, from Aisha

notes.t: Believers are told elsewhere in almost the same words not to forbid the good things Allah has made lawful to them; here the Prophet is the one asked the question first.

Tuḥarrimu and aḥalla sit on either side of the same root pair, ḥ-r-m against ḥ-l-l, that marks forbidden off from permitted through the rest of the Law; the verse opens on that boundary being moved by a person rather than by revelation.

2.sense: Taḥillah names the legal way out of an oath, discharged by expiation rather than kept forever. The verse answers what was just asked: the vow made in the line before is not a permanent lock, since Allah has already legislated how such oaths are undone. It closes on two names, protector, then knowing and wise, without opening a new point.

notes.t: The general rule for releasing an oath, feeding or clothing ten of the needy, freeing a slave, or a three-day fast if none of those can be managed, is set out at length elsewhere.
Taḥillah shares its root with ḥalāl, lawful, the very word used against the Prophet in the line before; the release from the oath is put in the same family of words as what the oath itself concerned.

3.sense: The Prophet confides a statement to one of his wives, and she passes it to another; Allah then lets him know that his confidence has been broken. He confronts her with part of what she did and lets another part pass. When she asks how he found out, his answer names its source rather than a person: the Knowing, the Aware.

notes.t: The root n-b-a runs through the verse four times, told, told, told, told, so that the sentence itself becomes a chain of telling, the very thing it describes.

Exegetes differ on which wife kept the confidence and which broke it, and on what the statement concerned; the identification of the two as Aisha and Hafsa comes from a separate hadith of Umar and is carried over to this verse rather than named in it.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report the identification without full agreement on the content of the secret

notes.t: Allah's knowledge of what is spoken in confidence is stated directly elsewhere: He knows the secret and what is more hidden still.

links.why: the same two wives, still unnamed here, are addressed directly and told to repent

4.sense: Addressed to the two wives named only by a dual pronoun, the verse sets a condition and its answer: repent, because their hearts had already leaned toward the fault, or else stand against each other against him and find that he needs no one's backing. The list that follows rises step by step, Allah first, then Gabriel, then the righteous among the believers, then the angels, leaving him supported regardless of what the two of them choose.

notes.t: Umar ibn al-Khattab is reported identifying the Prophet's two wives at the revelation of this line as Aisha and Hafsa, supplying a name the verse itself withholds.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of Tafsir, from Umar ibn al-Khattab

notes.t: Some commentators read "the righteous of the believers" as pointing specifically to Abu Bakr and Umar, fathers of the two wives named in the hadith; others take the phrase as unrestricted, any righteous believer.
notes.src: reported in at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir without agreement

notes.t: Gabriel is named apart from the angels here, the way he is elsewhere, set apart from the class he belongs to rather than folded into it.

links.why: the incident these two verses are answering, where a confidence was broken and then made known
the same warning continues, naming what could follow if the Prophet divorced his wives

5.sense: The warning is carried further as a hypothetical held out to the wives collectively: if divorced, a replacement is described in nine qualities, moving from the general, submitting, believing, to the specific, previously married and virgin, so that no case is left uncovered. The list is not a comparison of persons but a description of what would be asked of anyone standing in that place.

notes.t: Exegetes read sāʾiḥāt two ways, those given to fasting, since fasting is elsewhere likened to a journey, or those who migrate for Allah's sake; most tafsir favor fasting.
notes.src: at-Tabari and Ibn Kathir, with fasting the majority reading

notes.t: Qānitāt, devoutly obedient, is the same word used for righteous wives elsewhere, part of a settled vocabulary for describing them.

6.sense: The address widens from the Prophet's household to every believer, and the command is protective: guard yourselves and your families. The fire is described by its fuel, people and stones, and the angels set over it are given only two qualities, hardness and force, and a single trait beyond them, that they never act outside what they are told.

notes.t: The same phrase, a fire whose fuel is people and stones, is used earlier to describe the Fire prepared for the disbelievers.
Ghilāẓ describes a coarse texture, the opposite of soft, and shidād describes a strength that does not give way; neither word is about temperament, both are about refusing to bend.

7.sense: The address flips from believers to disbelievers, and the day named is the one the fire of the previous verse was prepared for. The command not to make excuses assumes excuses will be offered and turned away before they are finished, and the reason given closes the matter: payment matches only what was done.

notes.t: The same refusal of excuses on that day is stated elsewhere, a Day on which the guilty are not even given leave to speak.
Taʿtadhirū is the reflexive form of the root behind ʿudhr, excuse; the verb is built as an attempt made for oneself, which is exactly what the verse forecloses.

8.sense: Naṣūḥ describes a repentance thorough enough to close like a well-fitted seam, and the verse pairs it with a scene of light running ahead of believers and beside their right hands on the day the Prophet and those with him are not disgraced. The prayer that ends the verse, asking for the light to be completed, implies that even a granted light can still be partial, still needing something more at the end.

notes.t: The same scene, light running before believers and on their right while the Day is described in gardens beneath which rivers flow, is given at length earlier, alongside the hypocrites who ask to share it and are turned back.
Naṣūḥ is built on the same root as naṣīḥa, sincere counsel, and carries the older sense of a seam sewn tight, a repentance that closes a tear rather than covering it.

A hadith has the Prophet asked what sincere repentance is and answering that it is regret for the sin, seeking forgiveness for it, and resolving never to return to it; the chain carrying it is discussed.
notes.src: Ibn Majah, from Ubayy ibn Kaʿb; chain disputed

links.why: the fire that opened this run of address to the believers, answered here by light instead

9.sense: The address returns to the Prophet directly, the way it opened the surah, and gives one command toward two groups distinguished elsewhere only by what they profess outwardly. The same line, word for word, appears earlier addressed to the same command against the same two groups.

notes.t: This verse repeats an earlier one addressed to the Prophet almost word for word.
Jāhidi comes from the root behind jihad, effort; the verb itself does not specify by what means, only that it is demanded.

10.sense: Ḍaraba mathalan, struck an example, opens a pair of verses that will set two examples against each other, disbelief first. Marriage to a righteous man, even a prophet, carries the two women nowhere; what is emphasized is that kinship saves no one who does not believe.

notes.t: Lot's wife is told to leave with her household and excepted alone from the party, because she will be struck by what strikes the town behind her; the same exception is given more than once.

Khānatāhumā, betrayed them, is read by most exegetes as betrayal in belief and conduct, not marital infidelity, since both prophets are elsewhere described as faithful in delivering their message; a minority reading against this is rejected by the majority of commentators.
notes.src: Ibn Kathir and others reject an infidelity reading

notes.t: The same opening formula, Allah struck an example, opens the next verse too, pairing this example of disbelief against its opposite.

11.sense: The second example answers the first, belief against disbelief, and this one is given a voice, a prayer rather than a report. She asks for a house, not a husband, and names distance from Pharaoh three ways, from him, from what he did, and from the people who did it with him.

notes.t: A hadith names her, together with Mary, as the only two women to have reached complete faith, where many men reached it.
notes.src: Bukhari, Book of the Prophets, from Abu Musa al-Ashʿari

notes.t: The same woman appears elsewhere pleading for the infant Moses to be spared rather than killed.
Ibni, build, is the imperative for construction, not a general word for giving; she asks for an act, not a gift.

12.sense: The surah's third example completes the pair begun two verses earlier, moving from a wife defined by the man she asked to be saved from to a woman defined by guarding herself and by belief, with no husband named at all. The breathing into her recalls the same phrase used for the shaping of Adam, life entering matter directly from Allah.

notes.t: The same phrase, breathed into him of Our spirit, describes the making of Adam.
The fuller account of the news given to her, the angels speaking to her and her question about how, given that no man had touched her, is told at length earlier.
Al-qānitīn carries the masculine plural ending even though it describes Mary alone here; the form marks a general class of the obedient rather than a grammatical gender.
